finding.claim: update_doc calls can_edit() but discards the boolean result instead of calling require_edit(), so the authorization check is never enforced. Any caller can overwrite the body of any document. The sibling endpoint update_title correctly uses require_edit.
finding.source: Any request to PUT /doc/<doc_id> with a JSON body {"body": ...}. The attacker needs no ownership or editor rights. The doc_id comes from the URL path.
finding.sink: doc["body"] = request.json["body"] at docs.py:20, a write to the shared DOCS store.

trace.note: Route PUT /doc/<doc_id> is registered with no auth decorator.
doc = DOCS[doc_id] loads the target document by the attacker-supplied id.
can_edit(g.user, doc) returns False for a non-editor, but the return value is ignored, so no abort(403) happens.
The document body is overwritten with attacker-controlled data.

finding.guards_checked: Compared with update_title (docs.py:27), which uses require_edit and aborts with 403. There is no before_request hook or decorator in this file. can_edit (docs.py:7) is a pure predicate with no side effects. g.user is never set in this file, so authentication must come from elsewhere, and in either case the authorization check is not enforced. Minor related issues: DOCS[doc_id] raises KeyError (500) for unknown ids, and request.json["body"] raises KeyError when the key is missing.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: can_edit (docs.py:7) is a bool predicate whose result is discarded at docs.py:19; require_edit (docs.py:11) aborts 403 but is only used in update_title (docs.py:27). No decorator or before_request hook in the file.
verdict.reason: docs.py:19 calls can_edit() as a bare statement with the result discarded, so docs.py:20 overwrites doc["body"] for any caller, while update_title at docs.py:27 correctly uses require_edit; the attacker only needs to reach the PUT route (any user, or anonymous if g.user is unset elsewhere).
